teach: From the lesson: the three flags that plant a story in the past.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Ayer is the flag for the whole day that just finished: ayer trabajé — yesterday I worked — and we will build that sentence together very soon.' Another way: ayer opens the day in Bill's told story — ayer trabajé mucho.
walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson teaches three time flags: anoche, ayer, la semana pasada. (2) Anoche is the night and la semana pasada is the week. (3) The flag for the whole day that just finished, ayer, means: yesterday.

teach: From the lesson: trabajar in its past coat — the verb of Bill's day.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Trabajar — to work. And in the finished past, wearing the same faithful é coat: Trabajé — I worked.' Another way: ayer trabajé mucho — yesterday I worked a lot.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Trabajar means to work. (2) In the finished past, for I, it puts on the é coat and becomes trabajé. (3) Trabajé means: I worked.

teach: From the lesson: the night flag and the sleeping verb — a natural pair.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Anoche dormí bien — last night I slept well. Say it: Anoche dormí bien.' Another way: anoche closes the day that ayer opened.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Anoche means last night. (2) Dormí means I slept, and bien means well. (3) The whole sentence means: last night I slept well.

q: Which past-tense verb does Carmen call the rebel of the lesson?
teach: From the lesson: the one verb that refuses every coat.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Fui is fui — ir is the great irregular of Spanish, the rebel verb, and he is irregular in almost every language on earth' Another way: English did the same thing — go and went are strangers to each other too.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Hablé, comí and llegué all wear a past coat with an accented ending. (2) One verb refuses both coats and goes its own way. (3) That rebel, from ir, to go, is: Fui.

teach: From the lesson: llamar — the verb of lesson one — in its past coat.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Llamé a Jillian — I called Jillian. A — to, at — the little word Spanish puts before the person you called' Another way: hablé con Jillian is speaking with her; llamé is the call itself.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Llamar means to call, and llamé is I called. (2) The little a stands before the person called, as a courtesy. (3) The sentence means: I called Jillian.

q: Carmen teaches that verbs ending in ar, for 'I' in the finished past, land on one strong accented ending. What is that ending?
teach: From the lesson: the pattern your ear learns by noticing — hablé, llamé, trabajé, compré.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'if the verb ends in ar and the action is finished and it was you who did it, then the past coat ends in é, and your voice lands on that é like a period at the end of a sentence' Another way: the í ending belongs to the other family — comí, dormí.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Hablé, llamé, trabajé and compré are all ar verbs in the past, for I. (2) They share one landing sound at the end. (3) That shared, accented ending is: é.

teach: From the lesson: comer in the í family — the eating and sleeping verbs.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Comí bien — I ate well. Bien — well — from lesson nine's estoy bien — I am well. Say it: Comí bien.' Another way: ayer comí bien — yesterday I ate well.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Comer means to eat, and in the past for I it becomes comí. (2) Bien means well. (3) Comí bien means: I ate well.

teach: From the lesson: the widest of the three past flags.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'La semana pasada — last week. Semana — week. Pasada — past, gone by. La semana pasada: the week that has passed.' Another way: it stretches the same told story wider — la semana pasada trabajé mucho.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Semana means week. (2) Pasada means past, gone by. (3) Together, la semana pasada means: last week.

q: Bill wants to tell Jillian that he got home yesterday. What does he say?
teach: From the lesson: llegué a casa — the homecoming, the hinge of the day.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Ayer llegué a casa — yesterday I got home. Say it: Ayer llegué a casa.' Another way: everything before this sentence is the world; everything after it is home.
walk: Walk it through: (1) The flag for yesterday is ayer. (2) Llegué a casa means I got home. (3) Joined, his sentence is: Ayer llegué a casa.

q: Which sentence tells Jillian that Bill bought flowers for her?
teach: From the lesson: his telling at her table — true sentences, aimed at the listener.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Compré flores para ti — I bought flowers for you. Para ti — for you — ti, you, the word that turns a sentence toward the person listening.' Another way: compré is I bought, flores is flowers, and para ti puts them in her hands.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Compré flores says he bought flowers, but not who they are for. (2) Para ti means for you — it turns the sentence toward Jillian. (3) The sentence that tells her is: Compré flores para ti.

q: In your own words: what are the four moves Carmen teaches for building the nightly telling of your day?
teach: From the lesson: a frame that holds any true day you pour into it.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'We will build your telling from your own true yesterday, in four moves, and I will show you the moves so you can rebuild it every night with whatever the day actually held.'
walk: Walk it through: (1) Move one: plant the flag — ayer, anoche, or la semana pasada. (2) Move two: the work sentence — trabajé. (3) Move three: the people sentence — llamé or hablé. (4) Move four: the home sentence — llegué a casa, and anoche dormí bien if the night was kind.
